title: The Torch You Can Aim: Taking Hold of Attention
reflection: Ask often through the day: where is my attention right now, and can I move it? Notice where the beam is being pulled, then take one control back.

questions.q: Which three controls does Swamiji say the torch of attention has, each of which can be trained?
o: Brightness, aim and tuning, and steadiness of timing: the energy, where it points, and being in step.
Speed, length and width: how fast the beam moves, how far it reaches and how broad it spreads.
Memory, will and feeling: what the beam recalls, how hard it is held and how warmly it is felt.
Sight, sound and touch: the three senses by which the beam reaches the world around you.
questions.e: Brightness comes from how awake your body is and how much you care. Aim and tuning is matching the rhythm of what is there, like a radio dialled onto its station. Timing is being truly in step, like pushing a swing at the right moment. Focus harder gives no handle; these three do.
questions.c: Brightness, aim and tuning, steadiness of timing

questions.q: Sarah is ‘listening’ to her daughter on a worn-out evening and takes in nothing. Which control is she short of?
o: Timing only, since a tired person is always a little out of step with whoever is speaking.
Brightness: the torch is barely on, because real energy actually directed is what counts.
Aim only, since she plainly cannot be looking at anything at all while her daughter talks.
None of them, since a person who is tired cannot have a torch that she could train.
questions.e: Brightness is the energy you pour into looking, from an awake body and real care. You can be wired but scattered, or tired but riveted. In Sarah’s case the torch is barely on, and her daughter can feel the dimness.
questions.c: A tired evening is a dim torch

questions.q: Sarah is absorbed in a task and misses her son asking her something. How does Swamiji read this?
o: A spotlight doing what spotlights do, so the skill is to choose the beam the moment needs.
A sign she cares less for her son than for her work, which she should try to put right.
A fault of memory, since a good parent would always hear every word a child says to her.
A fault of the ears, which would be put right by sitting closer to her children at home.
questions.e: A torch can be a tight spotlight or a wide floodlight, but not both at full strength. Depth costs breadth. The answer is not guilt but choosing the beam the moment needs, and being able to widen it when something matters.
questions.c: Spotlight and floodlight cannot both be at full strength

questions.q: “A steady beam of attention also lowers the mind’s noise floor, while a jumping beam keeps it high.”
questions.e: A beam that jumps everywhere is itself scattered activity, which is noise. A beam that settles lets the floor drop, so quiet things become perceptible. The steady beam and the quiet mind are the same achievement from two sides.
questions.c: A steady beam lowers the floor

questions.q: What does the lesson say about how much of what you ‘see’ comes from the world?
o: Almost all of it, since the senses simply record whatever is in front of you without any addition.
None of it, since the whole of what you see is a forecast that your mind makes up on its own.
A great deal of it is the mind’s guess about what comes next, and the senses return the difference.
Only what you look at directly, since the edges of the visual field are always filled in by the mind.
questions.e: The mind constantly guesses what is about to happen from everything before, and the senses mostly send back the difference between the guess and what is really there. The question in any moment is how much weight attention gives to the guess and how much to what is in front of you.
questions.c: You largely see your prediction, not the world

questions.q: A patient reads a colleague’s neutral email as a threat. What does the lesson suggest Dr Watson does?
o: Argue her out of the fear with facts, until she accepts that the email was meant kindly.
Tell her to stop thinking about it, since the thought only has power if she goes on feeding it.
Notice the forecast as a forecast, then look together for what is actually present in the words.
Advise her to avoid the colleague, since the worry is a sign that something is wrong between them.
questions.e: In anxiety the beam is locked onto the forecast, and contradicting evidence arrives faint because little attention is left to receive it. You do not argue the fear away. You re-aim, and the experience changes because the weight of attention has moved.
questions.c: Notice the forecast, then re-aim at what is present

questions.q: A patient is in a low, flat state and cannot ‘look at the positives’. What order does Swamiji suggest?
o: Raise the brightness first through the body, such as movement, breath and rest, and then re-aim.
Re-aim first with firm encouragement, since the energy to do it will come once the patient tries.
Leave the patient alone until the mood lifts, since neither body nor mind can be helped meanwhile.
Offer a long talk on why things matter, since the forecast of nothing matters is simply wrong.
questions.e: In low states the beam is locked on a nothing-matters forecast and its brightness has collapsed, so it is too dim to move on command. The body comes first: gentle movement, breath, a change of posture. This sits alongside proper care, never in place of it.
questions.c: In low mood, raise the brightness first

questions.q: “A mind that holds its beam rock-steady on a fearful conviction is by that very fact freer than before.”
questions.e: Aim must walk with clear seeing. A steady beam held on a false story only makes you more certain of it. A focused mind pointed at its own fearful conviction is more trapped, a sharper prison. Discernment has to travel with steady attention.
questions.c: Steadiness without clear seeing is a sharper prison

questions.q: Kai picks up his phone to check one thing and surfaces twenty minutes later. What does Swamiji suggest he does?
o: Resolve never to touch the phone again, since any use of it means handing the torch over.
Watch the torch being yanked and name it, then take one control back, such as three breaths.
Blame himself firmly each time, since shame is what will make him put the phone down.
Leave things as they are, since the phone is built to win and no one can do anything about it.
questions.e: Every ping is a hand reaching for your beam. The designers are not villains; they use what is known about attention. The remedy is nothing exotic: see the hand, name it, and take one control back, without scolding. The torch was always Kai’s to hold.
questions.c: See the hand on the torch, then take one control back

questions.q: James is asked to choose his beam on purpose for one stretch of the day. What does he do?
o: Keep the beam wide all day, since feeling the whole room is the one mark of a good teacher.
Keep the beam narrow all day, since depth with one pupil is the one thing that really counts.
Let the day scatter the beam as it will, and only watch afterwards where it happened to go.
Pick one stretch for a tight spotlight and one for a wide floodlight, and notice that he chose.
questions.e: James has never framed it as a choice before. The point is that he chooses deliberately, instead of being scattered by default.
questions.c: Choose spotlight or floodlight on purpose
